identification: Kasia, Matha Kuar ka Kot (Gorakhpur district), kept for Kusinara but left open
evidence: Vogel keeps Kasia against V. A. Smith's Nepal Tarai site, but whether it is Kusinara is left for further excavation to decide.

Vogel's first Kasia season found a Kusana-period temple under the Nirvana temple, a 5th-c. inscribed terracotta Buddha, a stupa c. 90 ft square E of the temple and a monastery; no pillar on the eastern mound, so Carlleyle's site for Xuanzang's pillar is not confirmed.

At Sarnath the Jagat Singh stupa is of brick, not stone, and the main shrine is late (9th-c. inscriptions in its foundations), so Marshall doubts Oertel's equations with Xuanzang's stone stupa and 200-ft vihara; the excavated column is c. 50 ft against Xuanzang's 70 ft.
The Chaukhandi stupa, 800 yds SW of the monastery, is identified with the great stupa Xuanzang places 2-3 li SW of the Deer Park monastery.
Stein's survey of Mount Banj found the remains of an important Buddhist sanctuary (ruins, red soil), taken as the place of the body-offering.
Sarnath is taken as the Deer Park; Jinaprabhasuri's Tirthakalpa names the place near Benares Dharmeksa, with a Bodhisattva sanctuary.
Dhamek is identified with the Bodhisattva (Maitreya) stupa from the name Dharmeksa in the Jain Tirthakalpa.
The Asoka column, dug to its foot 17 ft below the terrace, stood c. 37 ft above ground, polished, with lion capital and wheel; Xuanzang's 70 ft is put down to his unreliable heights.
Dhamek is taken as the memorial where Maitreya received the prediction: solid stone to 36 ft 9 in, Cunningham's 1835 shaft found no relics, main niche faces W.

Chaukhandi, excavated, has three square terraces c. 12 ft high and broad with an octagonal plinth above, matching the "three robes, inverted bowl, staff" form of Xuanzang's 300-ft stupa 2-3 li SW of the convent; estimated height c. 200 ft.

identification: Kasia; identity with Kusinara left open
evidence: Marshall leaves the identity open and infers from the seals that Kasia may not be where the Buddha attained nirvana.
Vogel's 1905-06 season: sangharama wall c. 5,000 ft enclosing c. 36 acres, monastery L burnt c. end of 5th c., and numerous sealings of the monastery of the "Great Decease".
The Rajgir survey covered c. 35 sq. miles, with trial pits in New Rajagrha and a Hindu (Gupta) tower found in the old city.

identification: Kasia, undecided; town of Kusinara, if Kasia, between Anrudhva and Sisva, not at Anrudhva
evidence: Anrudhva digs found religious buildings (32-ft plinth, three small stupas) but no town; the seals may be imported letter-seals, so the identity with Kusinara stays undecided.
Clay seals (c. 400-900 AD) of the "Mahaparinirvana-vihara" show the Buddha's coffin between twin sal trees; they prove the site only if not imported letter-seals.
Two seals (c. 400 and c. 600 AD) belong to the convent of Makuta-bandhana, where the Buddha's remains were cremated.

identification: Old Rajagrha outer walls = Xuanzang's 150-li circuit
evidence: Marshall's survey: the outer walls along the hills to Giriak match 150 li at 6 li to the mile; the inner city walls are c. 4 miles.
Chhatha-giri was surveyed and climbed: Bimbisara's causeway from Udaya-giri with the two small stupas still on it, excavated (10th-12th-c. fragments).
Brick vihara ruins on the W precipice of Chhatha-giri, with a stupa below.

identification: stone watch-tower above the hot springs on Vaibhara
evidence: The Pippala stone house is identified with the stone watch-tower above the hot springs on Vaibhara.

identification: gardens N of the old N gate; vihara probably under the mound with a Muslim saint's grave
evidence: Bloch's trenches in the garden mound found nine brick stupas on a concrete floor and creed tablets of the 10th-11th c.

identification: possibly a plinth at the foot of Vipula behind the Suraj Kund
evidence: The Ajatasatru stupa is tentatively placed at a plinth at the foot of Vipula behind the Suraj Kund.

identification: artificially levelled spur on the N face of Vaibhara c. 1 mile W of the Pippala house
evidence: The spur, a little over a mile (5 or 6 li) from the Pippala house, has a pebble-paved terrace, ramps and cyclopean walls; Cunningham's Son Bhandar and Stein's Adinatha caves are rejected.

identification: deep ancient tank N of the Bamboo Garden
evidence: The deep ancient tank N of the garden is identified with the Karanda-hrada.
Cunningham's mound H for the Asoka stupa was trenched and showed Mauryan bricks reused under a Jaina statue.
A baked-clay seal-die "Sri-Vishnudvipa-vihare bhikshu-sanghasya" found E of monastery O makes Vogel think Kasia is Vethadipa, not Kusinara; Marshall does not consider the question settled.

The 1906-07 season found c. 500 clay sealings, 464 of the "Convent of the Great Decease"; the monastery doors face E as in Xuanzang's description; Ramabhar and the Matha-Kuar stupa remain unexcavated.

identification: Sarnath monastery = Saddharmachakra; Mulagandhakuti E of the Main Shrine
evidence: Seals reading "Sri-saddharmachakre mulagandhakutyam bhagavatah" and an 11th-c. inscription name the monastery; lamp-posts inscribed for the mulagandhakuti, found E of the main shrine, place the shrine of the colossal statue seen by Xuanzang there.

identification: Dharmarajika of the Mahipala inscription = Asoka's stupa
evidence: The Dharmarajika named in the Mahipala inscription is taken as Asoka's stupa.
The name Dhamekh is derived from an older dharmeksha.

identification: ancient Mathura = the elevated ground SW of the modern town, not the Katra
evidence: An extensive elevation of the soil SW of the town marks ancient Mathura; the Katra was the Yasa-vihara, and Cunningham's and Growse's identifications are rejected.
The Upagupta monastery (and the monkey tank) are still unlocated; Cunningham's Katra identification is rejected.

identification: Fleet's Kusinara near Pachrukhi (Saran): no supporting remains
evidence: A tour of Nov-Dec 1906 through Fleet's places found nothing supporting Kusinara near Pachrukhi.

identification: Fleet's Anoma crossing near Majhauli: no supporting remains
evidence: Anuaurpari ("across the Anuma") lies 4 miles from Majhauli, but no stream of that name (the channel is called Pusi) and no Buddhist remains were found.

identification: old town beginning c. 1.5 km before the 53 m Buddha, astride the road and river
evidence: Foucher's visits of 1922 and 1923 place the old town starting c. 1.5 km before the 53 m Buddha.
The 53 m Buddha serves as the landmark from which the old town is located.
The 35 m Buddha is stone finished in stucco; Xuanzang's 'brass' is explained as a metal sheathing in 630.
Ramparts, coins (Indo-Greek to Muslim), a stupa parasol and door jamb seen in 1923; the hostage monastery 3 li E fixes the site as the capital Xuanzang saw.
Begram, with two walled quadrangles (Burj-é-'Abdullah and a second 'royal city'), is the capital of Kapiśa.
An Eukratides coin restruck on Euthydemos, read 'Kaviçi' by Rapson, shows the city-goddess of Kāpiśī.

identification: the hill beside the city-goddess on the Eukratides coin
evidence: The goddess sits between a hill and an elephant protome, taken as the two sacred sites Xuanzang names near the city, supporting an early cult at the Pilu-sâr hill.

identification: Laghmān, reached from Kāpiśī by the direct road SE via Nijrâo, Tagâo and the Bâdpash pass
evidence: Foucher rode the route in Oct. 1925 (stupas along it, a marble liṅga at Tagâo); it is shorter and has only one pass.

identification: frontier of North India crossed on entering Lampāka
evidence: Xuanzang notes that on entering Lampāka he crosses the frontier of North India.

identification: Nagarahāra in the SW suburb of Jalalabad
evidence: The capital is placed where local tradition keeps an old 'Bégrâm', not at the Surkh-rûd confluence (Simpson).

identification: SW suburb of Jalalabad (old 'Bégrâm'), not the Surkh-rûd confluence
evidence: Located from two fixed points, the shadow cave (20 li SE) at Syâh-sang and Hi-lo = Hadda (30 li SE); given as provisional after six weeks in the field in 1923.
Marshall's excavations show no fewer than three successive Taxilas.
Of the three Taxilas, Sir-Sukh is the Kushan city, about as old as Purushapura; Foucher does not say which city Xuanzang saw.
Foucher leaves the second capital Hao-sa-la open for lack of fieldwork, noting that its spring should locate it with certainty.
Foucher doubts attaching the upper Helmand valley to Jāguḍa through its identification with Lo-mo-yin-tou.

identification: Śuna's temple where the Helmand leaves the mountains
evidence: From Xuanzang's two passages on the god, read as Śiva, the later temple of Śuna in Jāguḍa is put where the Helmand leaves the mountains.

identification: summit shown to Xuanzang from afar at Kāpiśī
evidence: Mount Aruṇa, where the god once lived, was shown to Xuanzang from afar at Kāpiśī; no site is given.
The text's NW descent from the summit favours the Khāvak pass, approached from Paghman N past Istâlif, Opîân, Tutam-Darrah, Parvân and Gul-behar.
The descent from the pass led into the Andar-âb valley.
The 12th-c. Kumaradevi inscription from Sarnath names the Dharmachakrajina image and the Dharmachakra-jina-vihara.
Cunningham identified Maheth with Sravasti; V. A. Smith placed it in Nepal between Balapur, Karhdi and Intava; the 1907-08 dig was to settle the dispute.
The Kushana inscription of Friar Bala on the colossal Bodhisattva found by Cunningham names Sravasti and the Kosamba-kuti; Hoey found a Vidyadhara inscription of 1119 and seals.
The Govindachandra plate settling Saheth as the Jetavana consequently settles Maheth as Sravasti, against V. A. Smith's Nepal site.

A copper plate of Govindachandra (A.D. 1130), found under the floor of cell 23 of Convent No. 19 at Saheth, grants six villages to the friars of 'the great convent of the holy Jetavana'; some villages still bear their names.

identification: Takht-i-Bahi not mentioned by the pilgrims
evidence: Spooner, following Foucher, notes that the Chinese pilgrims do not mention Takht-i-Bahi.
The Govindachandra copper plate establishes the identity of Saheth-Maheth with Sravasti.
The Govindachandra plate (Samvat 1186) was found in a cell of the SW monastery at Saheth.

identification: E mound of Shah-ji-ki-Dheri outside the Ganj Gate of Peshawar
evidence: Foucher's identification, tested by Spooner's 1908-09 excavation, rests on two mounds placed as in the pilgrims (stupa E, monastery W); Cunningham had earlier put Kanishka's monument at Gor Katri.

identification: the great W mound at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri
evidence: The monastery is the W mound, W of the stupa as in the pilgrims; a Sappers and Miners' dig of 1875 found Buddhist remains burnt by fire.

identification: to be sought by the octagonal Hindu temple N of the site
evidence: The pipal tree is to be sought near an octagonal Hindu temple N of the site.
A fourth inscription from Saheth confirms Maheth and Saheth as Sravasti and its Buddhist establishment.
A fourth inscription at Saheth (a Mathura sculptor's Bodhisattva) names Sravasti and the Jetavana.

identification: E mound at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri, outside the Ganj Gate, Peshawar
evidence: The relic chamber held a bronze casket inscribed 'Agisala, overseer of works at Kanishka's vihara in the sangharama of Mahasena', a crystal reliquary with three bone fragments and a coin of Kanishka.
Definite traces of the gigantic monastery Xuanzang speaks of were found W of the stupa; the casket names Kanishka's vihara.
The inscription supplies further authentic evidence that Saheth-Maheth is Sravasti, now a settled fact.
A pre-Kushana Brahmi inscription on a Bodhisattva from Saheth records its gift by Kshatriya brothers of Mathura 'in the Jetavana of Sravasti'.
A 6th-7th c. inscription records renewal of the stucco and painting of the temple (prasada), which must be the present edifice.

identification: the high plateau N and W of the temple (unexcavated)
evidence: The inscription mentions a brass image in the monastery (vihara); its remains lie buried beneath the plateau N and W of the temple.
Bloch shows the Umbrella Staff inscription is identical with the epigraph on the large standing Bodhisattva, which names Śrāvastī.
The epigraphs leave no doubt about Cunningham's identification of Saheth and Maheth.

identification: the casket stupa at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri, Peshawar
evidence: The Kanishka casket, found in 1909 under the stupa with a coin of Kanishka, has a Kharosthi inscription naming the Vihara of Kanishka.

identification: beside the great stupa at Shah-ji-ki-Dheri
evidence: The casket inscription names the Vihara of Kanishka in the monastery of Mahasena and the Sarvastivadins, matching Xuanzang's Little Vehicle monks in Kanishka's monastery adjoining the stupa.

identification: monastery mound beside Kanishka's stupa, Shah-ji-ki-Dheri (Peshawar)
evidence: The casket inscription shows Kanishka's vihara built at or near the older monastery of Mahasena; portions of the larger monastery the pilgrims saw have been recovered.
The Kushana Bodhisattva inscribed 'in the Jetavana of Sravasti' confirms Maheth as Sravasti.

identification: Saheth = Jetavana, E gate where Cunningham put it
evidence: An early-Kushana concrete road leads to the E gate, Kushana coins were found in monasteries F and G; temple 2 = Gandhakuti, temple 3 = Kosambakuti.

identification: possibly near Bhitti village, 2.5 miles W(N) of Maheth
evidence: Bhitti is a small early town site with a 56-ft square brick stupa of Mauryan-size bricks to its N; the suggestion holds only with Beal's '16 li'.
Hargreaves' work found a cruciform base of 180 ft, a little stupa by the E steps and a monastery wall facing the stupa, compared with Xuanzang's account.
The Nirvana-chaitya copper plate and the 'Mahaparinirvana' sealings support Kasia as Kuśinagara.

identification: the stupa behind the Nirvana temple = the parinirvana caitya
evidence: A copper vessel with a copper plate deposited in the 'Nirvana-chaitya' by Haribala (donor of the Nirvana statue), with coins of Kumaragupta, and c. 4th-c. sealings 'Mahaparinirvana bhikshu-sangha' in building Q.

identification: Ramabhar stupa, nearly a mile SW of Kasia (Cunningham's cremation site)
evidence: Ramabhar is a Mauryan-brick circular stupa with a drum of 112 ft; a shaft to water level found no relics, so the cremation site is not decided.
The plate shows that by the mid-5th c. tradition held that the Buddha died at Kasia.

identification: the large stupa behind the Nirvana temple
evidence: The copper plate (Nidana-sutra in ink) deposited by Haribala, dated by coins of Kumaragupta to the 3rd quarter of the 5th c., names the stupa the Nirvana-chaitya.
Excavation of six mounds shows most shrines ruined long before the 7th c., and none of Xuanzang's traceable Gandhara routes passed Sahri-Bahlol.
The copper plate and the Mahaparinirvana clay seals strongly favour Kasia, though no document can finally settle it; the Anrudhwa mound was empty.
1911-12: Mauryan remains round the plinth of the Nirvana temple, and Gupta sealings 'Sri-Mahaparinirvana bhikshu-sangha' with wheel and deer from a well.
Unexplained structures S of the Ramabhar stupa may throw light on the proposed identification with Makutabandhana.

identification: Taxila (Sirkap, Chir Tope, Jhandial, Bir mound), c. 20 miles NW of Rawalpindi
evidence: Trial digs were made at the Chir Tope, Sirkap, Jhandial and the Bir mound.

identification: not Cunningham's stupa N of Jhandial
evidence: The stupa N of Jhandial is a round 3rd-c. stupa over a Scytho-Parthian one with Soter Megas coins, far too late for Asoka's head-offering stupa; a gold relic casket lay in Cunningham's spoil.
Spooner found the Kumrahar fragments to be a Mauryan pillared hall (8 rows of 10 polished Chunar-sandstone columns 15 ft apart), not the single Asoka column Waddell took for the pillar of Xuanzang.
A section of the fortifications at the SE corner of Sirsukh was of Kushan large-diaper masonry with round loopholed bastions; a 3rd-4th c. block lay in the city centre.
Trial digging at Bara Pahari, where the great Asokan stupas are supposed to lie, found two stupas of apparently Mauryan date on a lofty platform.
First trial trenches at Nālandā found a monastery wall over 200 ft long and inscribed seals.
Inscriptions of Chola-Mahārāja and Mangi-Chola (c. 9th c.) tie Xuanzang's Chuliye to the Early Cōḷas of Cuddapah.
Work at Nālandā continued: Site 1 shows a fifth, older monastery and a long N-S trench was cut through the western stupa row.

identification: Shahbazgarhi village, 9 miles ENE of Mardan (Peshawar district)
evidence: Asoka rock edicts lie on two rocks ¾ mile SE of the village, the Po-lu-sha of the pilgrims; the old Khyber-Taxila road ran S of the inscriptions.

identification: Mekha-Sanda hill NE of the village
evidence: A few hardly traceable foundations on the Mekha-Sanda hill mark the retreat of the exiled prince.
Bloch's (1903) and Spooner's (1912) excavations at Basarh yielded over 1,200 inscribed seals, one of the 3rd c. BC, and polished Mauryan stone.
The Kesaria brick stupa on a platform, assigned to the 1st c. AD, is identified with the stupa Xuanzang describes.
Nine levels were found in monastery 1 (c. 6th-12th c.) and the site 4 monastery was cleared; Cunningham's attribution of site 4 is reported, not tested.
Dikshit traces old embanked roads in Varendra connecting Paundravardhana (probably Mahasthana) with ancient localities.
Stated in passing in a museum note on a stele, without evidence.
Kushinagara is put in the same Nepalese territory as Rummindei, in passing and without evidence.

identification: capital = Mangali on the Mangal stream (Hazara district); stupa and sangharama = Kushan basements on hill 4,219 ft S of the city
evidence: Hargreaves (9 Aug 1923) found a potsherd area between the Mangal stream and a nala matching the 7-8 li circuit, and Kushan diaper basements on the hill a furlong SE taken as the stupa and monastery, though rather S than SW.
Hund (13 Jan 1924) has Gandhara walling, diaper walls under the Muslim fort, a stupa base and a Sarada inscription; the 20 li circuit is plausible as the Indus has cut away the S side.
Sahni's terracotta ye dharma sealing proves Buddhist monuments at Bilsar.
Marshall's Kharoshthi ladle from the Sirkap 'Mahal' names Tachhasila.

identification: Old Rajgir: outer fortifications on the surrounding hills
evidence: The traced circuit of the outer walls agrees with the pilgrim's 150 li (c. 25 miles); walls stand 12 ft high E and W of the Panganga pass, with bastions and ramps.
The Vaibhara tower, with battered walls and small cells at the base, is taken as the Pippala Stone House.
An aside on the life-scenes on Nalanda votive stupas places Kusinagara in the Nepalese Tarai, without argument.
An aside on the life-scenes on Nalanda votive stupas places the Lumbini Garden at Rummindei, without argument.

identification: Paharpur (Rajshahi district), one of the 'deva temples' of Pundravardhana
evidence: Sealings of the Somapura mahavihara of Dharmapala and a Gupta plate of 479 AD granting land to the vihara at Vata-Gohali under the Nirgrantha Guhanandi make Paharpur one of the deva temples Xuanzang notes in Pundravardhana.
Dikshit states that the identity of Nalanda has been established by monastic sealings.
Dikshit states that the identity of Sarnath has been established by monastic sealings.
Dikshit states that the identity of Kasia has been established by monastic sealings.

identification: Gridhrakuta hill with the Bimbisara road, Rajgir
evidence: The Bimbisara road and old caves on the Gridhrakuta hills were cleared.

identification: summit shrine and caves on the Gridhrakuta
evidence: Traces of a small cave c. 30 ft below and W of the main shrine on the summit, with signs of other shrines E of it.
Majumdar's Bengal exploration excavated the Medh mound near Mahasthan, the ancient capital of Pundravardhana.

identification: Begram at the confluence of the Ghorband and Panjshir rivers (Foucher)
evidence: A Kharoshthi inscription on a bas-relief from Begram (Konow) is the first found near Kapisi.
Clay sealings from Monastery 11 bear the legend Sri-Nalanda-mahavihare Arya-bhikshu-sanghasya.

identification: Gridhrakuta hill, Rajgir: two brick stupas half way up the Bimbisara road
evidence: Remains of two ancient brick stupas in the middle of the Bimbisara road half way up the hill were cleared.

identification: brick shrine on the summit; caves near the top
evidence: The summit brick shrine yielded inscribed clay sealings of the Eight Buddhas, beads and a red-stone Buddha in dharmacakra-mudra; traces of shrines and a stone-paved path lie E and S of the caves.

identification: Basarh and adjoining villages (Muzaffarpur); palace = fort Raja Bisal ka garh
evidence: A survey of c. 12 sq. miles; the fort (c. 1,700 x 800 ft) has buildings back to at least 300 AD and c. 700 clay seals of the 4th-5th c.; village names Basarh = Vaisali, Baniya = Vaniyagrama.

identification: Lion pillar, brick stupa and Ram-Kund in mauza Kolhua
evidence: The Kolhua group, a little over 2 miles NW of the fort, has the lion pillar, a stupa N of it and the brick-faced Ram-Kund tank S, taken as the monkey-tank; its direction and distance tally with Xuanzang.

identification: 1 mile NW of the palace, now level fields (old silted tank)
evidence: Bloch could not find the relic stupa; the area 1 mile NW of the palace is now level fields.

identification: 1 mile NW of the palace, now level fields (old silted tank)
evidence: The Sammatiya monastery is placed with the relic stupa 1 mile NW of the palace, where no remains survive.

identification: five stupas = Panch Pahari (Bara and Chota Pahari), S of the Agam Kuan, Patna; possibly all five in the Bara Pahari mound
evidence: The Bara Pahari excavation found a wheel-plan stupa on an artificial kutcha-brick plinth and a second stupa SW of it, with Mauryan polished stone fragments and large bricks, confirming Waddell's identification.

identification: Baragaon ruins, 7 miles N of Rajgir
evidence: A trench across Cunningham's quadrangles 2 and 1 found the N wall of the southern monastery; Xuanzang's account was used to take quadrangle 1 as the oldest.

identification: Mahasthangarh, 7 miles N of Bogra, on the Karatoya
evidence: The fort and mounds were visited and city limits traced to Ram Shahr; Cunningham's identification, supported by the late Karatoya Mahatmya, is reported as not universally accepted.
The remains at Bhasu Bihar described by Cunningham were visited; no new evidence.

identification: Basarh and adjoining villages (Muzaffarpur); palace = fort Rājā Bisāl kā Garh N of Basarh
evidence: The fort keeps the name Visāla and its circuit of just under 5,000 ft agrees with Xuanzang's 4-5 li for the palace; a survey of c. 24 sq. miles was mapped.

identification: Lion pillar, stūpa and monkey tank (Rām-kund) in mauza Kollua E of Bakra, c. 2 miles NW of the fort
evidence: The Lion pillar stands 30 ft 6 in above ground, with a brick stūpa N of it (12th-c. inscribed crowned Buddha) and the Rām-kund (200 x 100 ft).

identification: 1 mile NW of the palace, traces gone (depression E of Baniya)
evidence: Bloch could not find the relic stūpa; only a depression E of Baniya marks the area.

identification: 1 mile NW of the palace, traces gone (depression E of Baniya)
evidence: The Saṁmatīya monastery is placed with the relic stūpa 1 mile NW of the palace, where its traces are gone.

identification: S of the city (Bloch, against V. A. Smith)
evidence: Bloch puts Āmrapālī's garden S of the city, rejecting V. A. Smith's placement.
An excavation 100 ft square round the Kosam pillar, and a Nagari inscription of Samvat 1245 from Meohar confirming Cunningham's Kosam = Kausāmbī.

identification: Thanesar; its Asoka stūpa possibly one of the mounds near Thanesar (Cunningham)
evidence: Repeats Xuanzang's three monasteries and Cunningham's proposal for the stūpa, which is not located.

identification: Kurukshetra mounds (Amin, Raja Karn ka Kila 2 miles from Thanesar), unexplored
evidence: Kurukshetra mounds are listed but none explored.
1935-36: a Deer-and-Wheel sealing with the Pala legend Sri Na[landa?] Dharmapaladeva (tentative reading), a Gupta sealing and coin moulds of Narasimhagupta Baladitya.

identification: old Rajagriha (Kusagarapura) = the hill-girt city of Rajgir
evidence: The Maniyar Math in the centre of the old city was dug 12 ft below the 1908 structure, showing two earlier, pre-Christian strata.

identification: New Rajagriha close to the old city on the N
evidence: New Rajagriha, founded by Ajatasatru, is placed close to old Rajagriha on its N.
Xuanzang saw the stone pillar on the site of the Migadaya, and the edict pillar was found at Sarnath.

identification: Oertel's edict pillar = the 70-ft pillar before Asoka's stupa
evidence: Oertel's broken polished pillar with Asoka's edict and a lion capital with wheel stood c. 37 ft above ground, so Xuanzang seems to have overestimated its height; the edict itself does not name the place.
Asoka's inscription says the king visited 'because the Buddha Sakyamuni was born here' and exempted the village of Lummini from taxes; Lummini and Rummindei are taken as the Lumbini grove.
The pillar's shaft is split and its horse capital lost (Mukherji); Xuanzang's river of oil is the present Tilar-nadi.
Takshasila, a provincial seat under Asoka, is identified with Shahdheri after Cunningham.

identification: Jaugada (Ganjam), whose district seat was called Samapa under Asoka
evidence: Separate edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada belong to Asoka's Kalinga; the head-quarters of Jaugada's district was Samapa; nothing on the 7th century.

identification: Tirath village on the border of Swat Kohistan
evidence: A boulder with two large footprints and an 11-letter Kharoshthi inscription of c. the mid-1st c. BC, found by Sir Harold Deane, matches Xuanzang's stone on the N bank of the Swat 30 li SW of the spring.

identification: near the head of the Swat at Kalam (Deane)
evidence: Placed from Xuanzang's distance of the footprint stone 30 li SW of the spring.

identification: Sirkap the chief settlement of Taxila in the Saka period
evidence: The Patika plate's locality Kshema, to the NE of the city, cannot be identified.
Stein showed the Mount Banj remains to be the site of the body-offering to the tigress; a Kharoshthi inscription from Mount Banj names a Vajra-stupa, though not the jataka.
Xuanzang's 200-ft Asoka stupa N of the spot is quoted; either of the two stupas may have been the Vajrastupa.

identification: E Mymensingh and Dacca E of the Brahmaputra, Sylhet, Tippera, Noakhali; capital Badkamta 12 miles W of Comilla (Bhattasali)
evidence: Bhattasali identified Samatata from Xuanzang's data (E of Tamralipti, S of Kamarupa, on the sea) and the Baghaura image inscription; the Allahabad pillar names it as a frontier state.
The Allahabad pillar names Kamarupa among the frontier states.

identification: Pundravardhana = Mahasthan, Bogra; Kotivarsha = Bangarh, Dinajpur
evidence: The Damodarpur plates name the Kotivarsha vishaya in the Pundravardhana bhukti.
Bloch's adhikarana seals at Basarh are cited.

identification: Pushpapura/Kusumapura = Pataliputra = Patna, originally at the old Son confluence (now near Dinapore)
evidence: Verse 7 of the Allahabad pillar names Pushpa as Samudragupta's capital.

identification: Kanauj, whose old name was Kusumapura
evidence: Xuanzang says the old capital of Kanyakubja was originally called Kusumapura.
A Mauryan fragment picked up in the ruins of Mahasthan names a royal granary at Pundranagara; the Karatoya-mahatmya lists Mahasthan's holy spots as Pundra-kshetra.

identification: Bhasu Bihar, 4 miles W of Mahasthan (Cunningham)
evidence: Cunningham found the Buddhist remains at Bhasu Bihar to correspond in description and position with Xuanzang's monastery.

identification: Surashtra = Kathiawad; Girinagara (Junagadh) at the foot of Urjayat
evidence: Skandagupta's inscription on the Asoka rock at Junagadh puts the town at the foot of Mount Urjayat.
Skandagupta's inscription at Junagadh names Mount Urjayat.

identification: Thanesar kingdom as described by Xuanzang, probably incl. parts of the S Panjab and E Rajputana (Cunningham)
evidence: The king's possessions probably did not go beyond the kingdom of Thanesar that Xuanzang describes.
The Patika plate records a relic and monastery at Kshema NE of Takhasila.
Takhasila is identical with the modern Sir-Sukh, a site covered with Buddhist ruins.
The Asoka pillar's inscription, 'here Buddha Sakyamuni was born', with the village Lummini, fixes the Lumbini garden with certainty.
The pillar was dug out 3 ft below ground; four stupa ruins lie near it and pilgrims' records of c. AD 800 are on the visible shaft.

identification: ruins 18 miles NW of Paderia between Amauli and Bikuli and Ramghat on the Banganga (Führer)
evidence: The country of the Sakyas has been sought too far S by Cunningham and his assistants; Führer's description of the ruins is not reliable.

identification: to be sought in the E Nepal Tarai, not at Kasia
evidence: If the Chinese bearing 'east of Lumbini' is right, Kusinara cannot be Kasia, where Cunningham and Carlleyle placed it.
Führer reports the birthplace of Krakucchanda and his 80-ft nirvana stupa one yojana SW of Kapilavastu, as in Faxian (later exposed as his invention).
The Nigliva edict records that Konakamana's stupa was enlarged in Asoka's 15th year.
Sasanka, king of Karnasuvarna, appears as overlord in Ganjam plates of AD 619-20; the capital is not located.
The Ganjam plates of AD 619-20 of the Sailodbhava Madhavaraja II are dated under Maharajadhiraja Sasankaraja.
Harsha's Madhuban plate of AD 631 was issued from the camp at Kapitthika, attesting the name.
The Madhuban plate names the Sravasti-bhukti, called after Sravasti.

The lower shaft is in situ with a Persepolitan lion capital carrying a wheel; the inscription had been covered by superimposed concrete floors (Oertel), which Vogel uses to explain Xuanzang's account.
Kushan Bodhisattva statues inscribed 'Sravasti' and 'Jetavana of Sravasti' confirm Maheth, against V. A. Smith's site near Balapur in the Nepal Tarai.
A copper plate found in 1908 in an earthen box in a cell of monastery 21 at Saheth names the Jetavana.
The Nidhanpur plates of Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa were issued from his camp at Karnasuvarna; the capital is not located.
Shih-li-cha-ta-lo is equated with Srihatta on the name; 'Srihattadhisvarebhyah' added above the Lakkha Mandal prasasti is adduced for it.
Kamalanka is identified with Comilla after Watters and Smith.
The eight chief villages of Hashtnagar, where a Buddha pedestal of the year 384 was found, occupy the site of ancient Pushkalavati.
Peshawar is named in passing as the Gandhara capital of Xuanzang's day.
The silver scroll from the Dharmarajika names Takshasila.
Boyer is inclined to identify the dhamaraia of the silver scroll, the Chir stupa, with Xuanzang's Kunala stupa; Konow does not decide.
Inscriptions of 1182 and 1234 at the Amaresvara temple in Amaravati name the city Sri-Dhanyakataka with its lofty caitya.
Chanda finds Xuanzang's reference to the great Chaitya of Amaravati ambiguous.

identification: stupa between Ghaligai and Shankardar on the Swat (Deane)
evidence: Deane identifies Uttarasena's stupa with remains between Ghaligai and Shankardar; the Kurram casket naming Ucharsana, equated with Uttarasena, is of unknown find-spot and adds no evidence of location.
Successive excavations at the Buddhist ruins near Kasia have shown them in all probability to be the ancient site of Kusanagara.
A Kalachuri stone inscription was found by Carlleyle in 1875-76 at the door of the brick shrine of the Matha Kuar image; it does not name the place.
Ikshvaku-period inscriptions at Nagarjunikonda naming Puvasela raise the question whether its remains represent the ancient capital of Dhannakataka.

identification: Puvasela (Purvasaila) named in the Nagarjunikonda inscriptions
evidence: Inscription F at Nagarjunikonda names Puvasela, the Prakrit form of Purvasaila.
The Nagarjunikonda inscriptions name a vihara on Siripavata E of Vijayapuri.

identification: hills E of the capital of Dhannakataka (Xuanzang)
evidence: The Pubba-selika sect named in the Nagarjunikonda inscriptions is derived from the Pubbasela convent; the site is not fixed.

identification: hills W of the capital of Dhannakataka (Xuanzang)
evidence: The Apara-selika sect named in the Nagarjunikonda inscriptions is derived from the Aparasela convent; the site is not fixed.

identification: province from the S bank of the Mahanadi incl. N Ganjam; capital perhaps on the Salima = Salia river near Chilka
evidence: Sailodbhava plates naming Kongoda-mandala were found at Cuttack, Khurda and Ganjam; Sasanka's Ganjam plate puts the capital on the Salima.
A Mauryan Brahmi plaque found at Mahasthan orders the Mahamatra of Pundranagara to relieve a famine, placing Cunningham's identification beyond doubt.
Restates Cunningham's identification of the Po-shi-p'o monastery with Bhasu Bihar.
Xuanzang's numerous Nirgranthas in Pundravardhana are compared with the Paharpur plate of G.E. 159.
Sirpur is taken as the capital, from which Arang lies SW and Vengi due S.

identification: Bhringara-parvata near Arang, SW of Sirpur
evidence: An ancient Brahmi stone inscription at Arang names Bhaimgara-pavata, and Arang lies SW of Sirpur as the pilgrim requires.
An inscription at Dharanikota reads ayirana Puvaseliyana negayasa, attesting Purvasaila monks there without fixing the convent's site.
The Purvasaila inscription found at Dharanikota itself supports the Amaravati-Dharanikota capital.
Xuanzang's Pi-lo-mo-lo, capital of Ku-che-lo, is Bhillamala, modern Bhinmal.
Ujjayini is treated as distinct from Malava.

identification: distinct from Ujjayini; Malava capital Vidisa (Bana)
evidence: Malava is kept apart from Avanti, with Bana's Vidisa as its capital.
Restates the Amaravati placing; no new evidence.
The Pubbasela sect named in a Nagarjunikonda inscription is supposed to derive from the convent Xuanzang places on the hills E of the capital.
The Aparasela sect named in a Nagarjunikonda inscription is supposed to derive from the convent Xuanzang places on the hills W of the capital.
A fragment of an Asokan pillar edict at Amaravati suggests the great stupa was Asoka's, though Xuanzang mentions no Asoka stupa at Dhanyakataka.
The pilgrim saw an Asoka stupa at the Kalinga capital, probably Kalinganagara, modern Mukhalingam.
The 1953-54 dig at the site called Jivakamravana found two building phases of elliptical halls with coarse red ware; no inscription.
The city rampart at Kausambi, c. 6th c. BC, was rebuilt thrice.
The Ghoshitarama, identified in 1951, was excavated: small stupas and an inscription of the nun Buddhamitra of Kanishka's reign.
Structures at Kumrahar from c. 150 BC were excavated.
Sirpur, capital of the Pandava dynasty of the 7th c., has a Saiva panchayatana temple excavated; not linked to Xuanzang.

identification: Bhinmal (Jodhpur) = Srimala, capital of the Gurjaras
evidence: Bhinmal, early medieval Gurjara capital, was excavated: medieval brick structures, dark grey and red-polished ware; not linked to Xuanzang.
The excavation of the Ghoshitarama at Kausambi was completed, with the adjacent E gateway of the city exposed.
Work at Kumrahar showed the nature, extent and destruction of the Mauryan palace at Pataliputra.
A Buddhist establishment at Sirpur with an 8th-c. inscription of Balarjuna was excavated.
Renewed excavation (1954-55) exposed another elliptical structure with two large halls and crude red ware; no inscription.
The rampart and the E gateway, with a mud-bund curtain, were excavated.
The plan of the Ghoshitarama was completed: massive square stupa, Hariti shrine, S boundary wall of 181 ft (Bhadramagha to 6th c.).

identification: Kumrahar = Mauryan pillared hall of Pataliputra
evidence: The 84-pillared hall at Kumrahar stood on wooden bases and was destroyed in the mid-2nd c. BC.
Stratigraphy at Pataliputra and a fragment of a probable Asokan pillar-capital.
Work in the Ghoshitarama was wound up with sixteen structural sub-periods over a thousand years.
At Kanauj Painted Grey Ware was found below NBP.
Two more monasteries were excavated at Sirpur.

identification: Ghoshitarama at Kosam; Main Stupa with an Asokan enlargement = the stupa Xuanzang ascribes to Asoka
evidence: The Main Stupa, built c. 5th c. BC, was enlarged in the 3rd c. BC, which the excavator ties to Xuanzang's Asoka stupa at the Ghoshitarama; occupation from c. 6th c. BC to the 6th c. AD, ended by the Hunas under Toramana.
The mound of ancient Kanyakubja has a 40-ft deposit from PGW to late medieval.
NBP-period remains, Mauryan polished pieces and a conflagration before 100 BC.
A 65-ft tower in the E rampart has five phases, and the rampart is earlier than NBP.
The Ghoshitarama yielded a standing Buddha in local sandstone and balustrade-pillars with Gaja-Lakshmi.
The Kausambi brick wall stood over 40 ft high.
The excavator thinks the pre-Mauryan stupa at Vaisali may be one of the eight stupas built over the Buddha's relics.
Rajghat, the site of ancient Varanasi, has NBP to medieval levels.

identification: small mound NE of Kharauna-pokhra, c. half a mile NW of Raja-Visal-ka-garh
evidence: The dig, guided by Xuanzang's location (NW of the city, SE of the Asoka pillar), found a mud stupa of NBP date enlarged four times, a soapstone relic casket only a quarter full in a breach in the core, and a second breach on the W side ascribed to the ruler who tried to rifle it; no inscription.
More elliptical structures were exposed; the long stone wall S of the road to Griddhrakuta is a reservoir bank.
PGW and pre-NBP ware occur in the lowest pre-fortification levels.
Painted NBP ware was found at Kausambi.
The Vaisali defences show three Periods.
The base of the despoiled Amaravati stupa was traced and relic-caskets found; the identification is not discussed.
A moat and road at the foot of the rampart, and iron before NBP.
A trench 126 x 15 ft across the N fortification of Mahet showed a long pre-defence occupation with PGW and pre-NBP ware, c. second quarter of the 1st millennium BC.
The fort has brick structures in three Periods, the earliest wall pre-Sunga, with seals and sealings bearing Brahmi legends.

identification: Asoka pillar at Kolhua, 3 miles N of the fort
evidence: Two mud stupas by the pillar (183 and 179 ft in diameter) were excavated, the northern with copper vessels, one holding relics 'presumably of a Buddhist saint'; not identified with Xuanzang's stupa.
Baniya has a single NBP period; NBP ware below the stupa near the Chaturmukha-Mahadeva temple was confirmed; Virpur has three periods.

identification: New Fort, Rajgir, outside the hill-girt valley (new city ascribed to Ajatasatru)
evidence: A 66-m cutting across the S defences found pre-defence habitation with NBP, iron and 14 punch-marked coins, ended by a conflagration, then a mud rampart with brick retaining wall and moat.
The early city-site of Tilaura-kot, N of Taulihawa, was excavated; the report does not identify it with Kapilavastu.
Lumbini yields grey ware and antiquities from the 3rd c. BC to at least the 9th c. AD.

identification: fortified township at Dharanikota, right bank of the Krishna (Guntur)
evidence: A cutting across the W side showed seven phases: six of an embankment-cum-wharf on a navigation channel, the last the defences; Dhanyakataka and Xuanzang are not named.

identification: beside the Raktamrittika monastery at Rajbadi-danga
evidence: The dig aimed at identifying Karnasuvarna, Sasanka's capital, whose suburbs held the monastery named on the sealing.

identification: Rajbadi-danga at Jadupur, over 1 km from Chiruti station (Murshidabad)
evidence: A Phase III (6th-7th c.) sealing names the Rakta-mrittika-mahavihara; Phase III has a platform and two circular basements probably of a stupa, with seals bearing the Buddhist formula.
Fort-wall phases, a reservoir bund (Hamsala-Gundam) with Rouletted and NBP wares, and the brick revetment of the navigation channel along the S wall; Dhanyakataka and Xuanzang are not named.
Supported by the monastery's identification, with Phase III dated to Xuanzang's time.
Sealings name the Raktamrittika-vihara and its acharya-bhikshu; seals are palaeographically 6th-10th c. (central date 7th-8th c.), C-14 for Phase III 1200 ± 80 BP.

identification: habitation area within the fortifications of Dharanikota (Guntur)
evidence: Habitation from the toe of the rampart in four Periods, from megalithic Black-and-red Ware to grey ware; Dhanyakataka and Xuanzang are not named.
Phases III-IV have a panchayatana temple-complex (enclosure 20.87 m, four corner shrines) beside the monastery; no new inscription.
The 1966-67 season sought the complete plan of the panchayatana temple-complex: enclosure walls of two phases with niches, square corner shrines, four structural phases.

The site, with the building pattern of a Buddhist monastery and seals of c. 5th-6th to 8th-9th c., is identified with Xuanzang's Raktamrittika sangharama on the strength of the seals and other remains.
Karnasuvarna, hitherto uncertain, is to be located in the neighbourhood of Rajbadidanga.
1968-69: seven trenches, three Periods; 25 seals read (personal names, one in 7th-8th-c. script, a Roman-letter seal), none naming the monastery.

identification: Rajbadidanga (Murshidabad) = locale of the Raktamrittika vihara
evidence: On the basis of the seal-inscriptions (5th-6th to 9th-10th c., mostly Phases 3-4) the site is firmly identified with the Raktamrittika-vihara of Xuanzang's accounts; occupation runs from the 2nd-3rd to the 12th-13th c.
The monastery stood in the neighbourhood of Karnasuvarna, the metropolis of the Gauda kingdom in the 7th c.
Wooden pillars in alignment, an ornamental stone pillar, Mauryan terracottas and NBP ware at Kankarbagh are taken as part of the Mauryan palisade.

identification: Ayodhya (coin of the city found there)
evidence: A copper coin with the legend Ajudhe in 1st-c. BC Brahmi, found at Ayodhya, shows a city of that name there; Xuanzang is not discussed.
The 1972-73 season yielded many inscribed seals, one reading "Sri Raktamrittika Mahavihara[ry]a-bhikshu Sanghasya", and monastery walls of Phases II-VI.
Several inscribed seals with Raktamrittika legends support identifying Xuanzang's Raktamrittika monastery with Rajbadidanga; occupation c. 4th-5th to 11th-12th c.

identification: Birdpur mound, 9 km S of Piprahwa, District Basti
evidence: The distance and direction from Piprahwa (as Kapilavastu) are said to fit Xuanzang's Sarakupa; the mound has two copper vessels at 6 m depth and an earlier stupa(?) of Kushan-Gupta date; no inscription.
The Birdpur identification measures the well's distance from Piprahwa, taken as Kapilavastu.
1981-82: the NE side of the gateway wall was traced towards the main monastery wall, with an earlier Period I platform and Phase II seals; no inscription reported.
1986-87: 41 burnt-brick structures in six phases on the S of the mound, occupation into the post-Gupta period (6th-7th c.), and a 'ye dharma hetu' sealing of c. 5th-6th c.
1987-88: a Kushana terraced tank W of the Gandhakuti shrine, a circular stupa with cells, a Kushana monastery and a Gupta temple; occupation 1st to 11th-12th c.
1988-89: a stupa over a Kushana cell, the terraced tank, Gupta temples and votive stupas; four periods from Kushana to Gahadavala.

identification: stupa and Asokan pillar complex at Kolhua
evidence: 1989-90: votive stupas W of the pillar-stupa complex, a Kushana-Gupta-post-Gupta monastery 80 m SW of the pillar facing the main stupa, ye dhamma plaques; the report does not cite Xuanzang.

identification: Kolhua: Kushana brick-lined tank by the pillar-stupa complex
evidence: The Kushana brick-lined tank by the pillar, c. 32.5 x 31.5 m with seven tiers and two bathing ghats, was fully exposed; the report does not link it to the monkey tank.
First stratified excavation: mounds within an earthen rampart of c. 6 km, Asokan elephant capital, PGW to Kushan sequence.

identification: Sankisa, the place of the descent from the Trayastrimsa heaven
evidence: Sankassa is the Pali place of the descent; a brick stupa mound lies 300 m S of the village under the Bisharidevi temple.

Second season: NBPW to Gupta occupation, a room W of the elephant-capital site probably part of a Maurya-Gupta monastery, and brick debris NE of the 'so-called Stupa mound' pointing to an important building.
The Kesariya stupa has five terraces with cells and a drum 9.38 m high and c. 22 m across.
A terraced brick stupa in a mound 200 m N of the SW gate of old Rajgir was excavated; it is not linked to Xuanzang.

identification: brick stupa in front of the Asoka pillar at Kolhua
evidence: Clearance in front of the pillar exposed a brick stupa 24.5 m in diameter and 7.5 m high; no reference to Xuanzang.

identification: Sarai mound E of the Nalanda remains
evidence: Sculptures, a 22 m niched brick wall, staircases and a 14-line prasasti were found at the Sarai mound.

identification: Taradih mound, Bodh Gaya: Gupta-Pala monastic complex
evidence: Gupta and Pala structures of a monastic complex with cells on a common verandah and Pala sealings with the Buddhist creed; not linked to Xuanzang.
Xuanzang's Rajapuri is modern Rajouri, subject to Kashmir; Kushan red ware at Kheora 1.5 km above Rajouri.
Xuanzang's Parnotsa is modern Poonch, subject to Kashmir; Kashmiri coins (8th and 11th c.) and temple ruins at Panjnara.
The stupa held three khondalite relic caskets with bone relics in gold caskets, so it might be the stupa noticed by Xuanzang.
